title: Saying No With Data and Discipline
description: Master the art of declining feature requests, managing scope creep, and avoiding sunk cost traps using data-driven frameworks.

interactions.prompt: Your B2B SaaS backlog: 142 feature requests. Top 5 enterprise clients generated 68% of revenue but submitted only 12 requests. The remaining 130 requests come from 340 SMB accounts contributing 32% of revenue. What's the critical signal?

options.text: SMB customers are more engaged and deserve proportional investment
Enterprise request density per dollar is dramatically lower—each carries outsized weight
You should ignore SMB requests entirely and focus on enterprise
The backlog is too large; freeze all intake immediately

chartData.title: Revenue vs Feature Requests by Customer Segment

interactions.prompt: Stripe's payments team has capacity for one initiative. Option A: a compliance feature required by EU regulation in 9 months, estimated 4 months of work. Option B: a checkout redesign projected to lift conversion 8%, worth ~$14M ARR. Your biggest enterprise prospect ($2.1M ACV) just made Option B a contract condition.

options.text: Build Option B—$16.1M total revenue impact justifies prioritization
Build Option A—regulatory deadlines are immovable, B can follow
Split the team 50/50 across both initiatives
Negotiate a phased Option B MVP to close the deal, then pivot to A

interactions.prompt: When triaging feature requests, the ____ framework scores each request on Reach, Impact, Confidence, and Effort to produce a comparable numeric priority score that removes emotional bias from scope decisions.

options.text: RICE
MoSCoW
Kano
WSJF

interactions.prompt: You're a PM at Figma. Rank these requests for a Q3 roadmap from highest to lowest priority: (a) CEO's pet feature for AI-generated layouts—no validated demand. (b) Critical accessibility bug blocking a $4.5M government contract. (c) API performance fix reducing p99 latency—tracked as top-3 churn driver. (d) Dashboard redesign requested by 40% of NPS detractors.

options.text: AI-generated layouts (CEO request, unvalidated)
Accessibility bug (blocks $4.5M government contract)
API latency fix (top-3 churn driver)
Dashboard redesign (40% of NPS detractors)

interactions.prompt: Your team spent 7 months and $1.2M building a recommendation engine. Post-launch: 3.1% adoption, 0.4% lift in conversion vs. the 5% target. A stakeholder proposes another $600K to "fix it." Engineering estimates the $600K has a 25% chance of hitting the 5% target. What matters most?

options.text: The $1.2M already spent justifies continued investment to recoup costs
Expected value of the $600K fix is $150K equivalent—kill it
3.1% adoption is a strong base to iterate from
Give the team one more quarter to prove the concept

interactions.prompt: Shopify's platform team tracks 47 points of accumulated tech debt. Addressing all of it requires 6 engineering-months. Meanwhile, a competitor just launched a feature that 3 of your top-10 merchants are asking about. Sales says you'll lose $8M ARR if you don't ship a response in 8 weeks. Your team has 4 engineers.

options.text: Ship the competitive response fast, accept more debt accumulation
Pay down debt first—velocity will increase for all future work
Triage debt: fix only items on the competitive feature's critical path, then ship
Hire contractors to handle the competitive response while the team fixes debt

interactions.prompt: You lead product at a Series C fintech. Rank these scope management actions from most to least impactful for protecting your Q4 delivery: (a) Add a 20% buffer to all engineering estimates. (b) Establish a formal change request board that meets weekly with cost-of-delay data. (c) Send a quarterly email reminding stakeholders not to add scope. (d) Define explicit "not doing" lists published alongside every roadmap commitment.

options.text: Add 20% buffer to all engineering estimates
Formal change request board with cost-of-delay data
Quarterly email reminding stakeholders about scope discipline
Publish explicit 'not doing' lists alongside every roadmap

interactions.prompt: Your CEO just personally promised the feature to a keynote audience of 2,000 people at your annual conference, with a "shipping next month" commitment. Engineering says it's 3 months of work minimum. How do you handle this?

options.text: Crunch the team to deliver in 1 month—CEO credibility is paramount
Ship a limited beta to conference attendees, buy time for full release
Tell the CEO to publicly retract the commitment
Descope to a thin MVP that delivers core value in 4 weeks

interactions.priorContext: You previously decided to kill the recommendation engine and reallocate that team. Now your CEO has publicly committed to a feature your freed-up engineers could theoretically build—but the timeline is impossible.
